title: The Teacher's First Test of the Day, Part 2 (Or How to Boost Your Credibility and Sanity with a Clear and Reinforced Start-of-Class Procedure)
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Following up on his alarm-clock post, Stuart applies the "first test" framing to the classroom: the question every student implicitly asks upon entering is "what do we do when we enter this classroom?" He argues that vague or absent answers to that question ("I dunno," "wait for the teacher to start things") waste hundreds of class minutes across a school year and slowly erode teacher sanity, while clear, consistently reinforced answers signal Competence, one leg of his Care-Competence-Passion credibility framework. He illustrates the point with three real start-of-class routines at increasing levels of specificity: Fred Rogers changing his shoes and sweater while singing, colleague Lynsay Fabio's tightly choreographed door-greeting-to-warm-up sequence, and Stuart's own more relaxed but still-structured routine of an always-posted warm-up and a visible countdown timer. He lays out a three-step implementation process — have a plan, teach and model it with specificity, and reinforce it especially early in the year — and points to several Michael Linsin classroom-management articles as further reading on the reinforcement step.
points: Stuart reframes classroom entry as a recurring "test" every student poses to the teacher, arguing that vague answers to "what do we do when we enter?" quietly cost hundreds of class minutes over a year.
He ties a clear start-of-class procedure directly to his Care-Competence-Passion credibility framework, positioning it specifically as a Competence signal rather than just a management tactic.

The three contrasting examples (Fred Rogers, Lynsay Fabio, and his own routine) show that a clear procedure doesn't require one specific style — it requires consistency and specificity, whether relaxed or tightly choreographed.
His three-step implementation model (plan, teach and model with specificity, reinforce especially early on) turns the idea into a repeatable process rather than a one-time announcement to students.
quotes: This is the question that our students first test us with, each and every time they come into the classroom. The testing isn't them being mean — it's them being a group of human beings.

When the answers to the question are "I dunno" or "Wait for Mr. Stuart to start things" or "Chat with my buds," we're probably not passing the test at all because we've not made a start of class procedure consistently clear.
This'll end up leading to hundreds of wasted class minutes over the course of the school year, and it'll also slowly but surely degrade our sanity — kind of serious things.
How did Fred Rogers do it? He walked into the house while singing a song, switching out his outside jacket and shoes for an inside sweater and pair of tennis shoes.
By the time the bell has wrung, you're in your seat and have quietly started on your warm-up, which is always posted on the screen in front of you.
